# PHYSICAL REVIEW C 111, 044608 (2025)

12C(n, n′ 1γ) partial γ-ray cross section measured using the GENESIS array

J. M. Gordon ,1,* B. L. Goldblum ,1,2 J. A. Brown,1 T. A. Laplace ,1 J. C. Batchelder ,1 D. L. Bleuel ,3

C. A. Brand,1,3 B. Buckley ,4 A. Georgiadou ,1 C. J. Henderson,1 T. S. Johnson ,1 J. W. Lee ,1

K. Myers ,1 T. S. Nagel ,1 J. R. Sebastian ,1 A. S. Voyles ,1 and L. A. Bernstein 1,2

1Department of Nuclear Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720, USA 2Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California 94720, USA 3Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, California 94550, USA 4Air Force Institute of Technology, Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio 45433, USA

(Received 11 October 2024; revised 7 February 2025; accepted 26 March 2025; published 18 April 2025)

Improved neutron inelastic scattering cross sections have repeatedly been identiﬁed as a top priority nuclear data need, important for basic science and a range of applications in nuclear energy, stockpile stewardship, and proliferation detection. For the 12C(n, n′γ ) reaction in particular, recent measurements have unveiled some structural discrepancies, demonstrating incongruities among themselves and in relation to the ENDF/B-VIII.0 nuclear data evaluation. To help resolve these disagreements, a measurement was performed at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory using a broad-spectrum neutron beam and a 99.8% pure natural carbon target. The Gamma Energy Neutron Energy Spectrometer for Inelastic Scattering (GENESIS) was employed to measure energy-differential γ -ray emission spectra as a function of incident neutron energy in the energy range of 5.5 to 16.7 MeV. The 12C partial γ -ray cross sections were extracted at 63◦, 122.5◦, and 150◦with respect to the incoming neutron beam and integrated using angular distribution data available in the literature. The data show agreement with a recent literature measurement and evaluation from 11 to 15 MeV, but indicate a larger cross section for incident neutron energies between 5.5 and 8.5 MeV. The measured relative angular distributions are also reported and were found to agree with evaluation.

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevC.111.044608

## I. INTRODUCTION

Neutron inelastic scattering cross section data are needed in the fast neutron energy range to support the design and development of next-generation nuclear technologies [1,2]. In the case of nondestructive assay, γ -ray emissions from active neutron interrogation provide a means for material identiﬁcation with isotopic speciﬁcity that is important for arms control, treaty veriﬁcation, emergency response, and controlled substance detection [3,4]. Modeling secondary neutron and γ -ray emission data is critical to the development of active neutron interrogation systems, as it enables the scoping of physics limitations, optimization of system design parameters, and development of robust analysis algorithms [5]. For 12C in particular, partial γ -ray cross section data are needed due to the prevalence of carbon in structural materials, controlled substances, and detector components [5]. However, inconsistencies amongst literature measurements of the 12C(n, n′γ )

cross section and discrepancies with the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation [6] warrant further study. In 2022, Ramirez et al. [7] measured the 12C(n, n′ 1) inelastic scattering cross section for incident neutrons in the energy range of 5.6 to 7.8 MeV. This work showed good agreement with the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation [6] and a measurement from Perey and Kinney [8], but notable discrepancies with other legacy literature data [9,10]. More recent work by Kelly et al. [11] extended this knowledge, measuring the shape of the 12C(n, n′ 1γ ) cross section from reaction threshold up to 16 MeV incident neutron energy. While these results trended well with the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation [6] and other literature data [12,13], some signiﬁcant structural differences were observed. Additionally, the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation found it necessary to rescale prior results from Wender et al. [12] and Negret et al. [14] in order to obtain consistency across the experimental data and with the calculated cross sections [6]. As such, there is still a need for experimental data with accurate and well-documented normalization. The angular distribution of the 4.439 MeV γ ray produced in the 12C(n, n′ 1γ ) reaction has also been studied. The most extensive datasets are from Wender et al. [12], who measured the distribution from threshold to 25 MeV at ﬁve angles between 40◦to 140◦relative to the neutron beam, and from Kelly et al. [15], who measured from 6.45 to 16.6 MeV at nine angles between 30◦and 150◦. Both authors report distributions that contain non-negligible ℓ= 4 Legendre polynomial

contributions in contrast to the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation which contains weighting factors up to ℓ= 2. To further inform the 12C(n, n′ 1γ ) cross section in the neutron energy range of interest for active neutron interrogation applications, the Gamma Energy Neutron Energy Spectrometer for Inelastic Scattering (GENESIS) was employed at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) [16]. The GENESIS array consists of both highpurity germanium (HPGe) CLOVER detectors and organic liquid scintillators, enabling the measurement of energy- and angular-differential neutron and γ -ray production cross section data over a broad energy range. This paper presents results from the HPGe detectors. Section II consists of a description of the experimental methods applied in this work, including details on the conﬁguration of the GENESIS array as well as HPGe energy and timing calibrations. In Sec. III, the methods for measurement and extraction of the neutron ﬂux spectrum are provided. Section IV describes the analysis of data collected using the GENESIS array for extraction of the partial γ -ray cross section. In Sec. V, the measured γ -ray production cross sections are presented and compared with previous measurements from Kelly et al. [11,15] and the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation [6]. Concluding remarks are given in Sec. VI.

## II. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS

The experimental study of the 12C(n, n′ 1γ ) reaction was conducted at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at LBNL using the GENESIS array. Neutrons were produced by impinging a 25 MeV 2H+ beam on a 3.5-mm-thick carbon breakup target in the cyclotron vault [17]. The breakup target was housed in a Faraday cup connected to a beam current monitor that recorded the current once per second. Due to the high cyclotron repetition rates and relatively short ﬂight paths at the LBNL facility, the neutron beam exhibits frame overlap whereby fast neutrons created from a given beam pulse arrive at experimental stations at the same time as slower neutrons from previous pulses [18]. For this experiment, the 25 MeV 2H+ beam resulted in a 127.236 ns cyclotron pulse period. Neutron beam production was performed on the opposing side of a 2.4-m-thick steel and concrete wall with respect to the experimental area and was additionally collimated on the far side of the wall using a tapered cylindrical copper collimator [16]. Neutrons entered the experimental area via a 10-cmdiameter iron beam pipe in the concrete wall and were made incident on a pressed graphite carbon target of 99.8% 12C elemental purity positioned at the center of the GENESIS array, 734.4 cm from the breakup target. The target was an elliptic cylinder, 1 mm in thickness, with a minor diameter of 76.2 mm, major diameter of 107.8 mm, and weight of 6.564 g, the latter determined using an analytical balance [19]. The major axis was oriented at an angle of 51.9◦relative to the incident neutron beam. Calculations based on the ENDF/ B-VIII.0 library [6] and the measured neutron spectrum yielded a multiple scatter probability of 1.231 ± 0.005%(stat.). Tuning of beam optics was managed using a two-dimensional raster scanning system, deployed downstream of the GENESIS array, which provided neutron counts

FIG. 1. GEANT4 rendering of the GENESIS array geometry in the experimental runtime conﬁguration. The neutron beam is incident from the upper right side of the schematic.

as a function of position using a 2.54 cm h. x 2.54 cm dia. right circular cylindrical EJ-309 scintillator [20] closely coupled to a Hamamatsu H6533 photomultiplier tube (PMT) [21]. Using this system, the collimator was conﬁgured to ensure uniform illumination of the neutron beam on the carbon target. Data collection was undertaken over a 10-day period with approximately 100 h of beamtime with the carbon target present at the center of the GENESIS array and approximately 10 h of beamtime in the absence of a target for background subtraction. The neutron ﬂux spectrum measurement was conducted over the duration of the beam time on target. Throughout the data collection period, several measurements of sealed sources were performed for calibration and model validation. A description of the GENESIS array including detector characteristics, instrumentation details, and methods for construction of event timing, gain calibrations, and detection efﬁciency modeling was provided in Gordon et al. [16,22]. For this experiment, three Eurisys two-fold segmented HPGe CLOVER detectors [23] and twenty-six 5.08 cm dia. x 5.08 cm h. right-circular cylindrical EJ-309 organic liquid scintillators with pulse shape discrimination capabilities [20] were included in the array. The EJ-309 cells covered an angular range of 11◦–165◦with respect to the incoming neutron beam and were positioned at a radial distance of approximately 0.45 m to 0.9 m from the carbon target. The CLOVER detectors were positioned in the horizontal plane of the beam at polar angles of 63◦, 122.5◦, and 151◦with respect to incident neutron beam direction. The angular coverage of the CLOVER detectors when operated in total detection mode [23] was 6.4◦, 4.5◦, and 4.7◦, respectively. A GEANT4 [24] rendering of the geometry speciﬁc to this experiment is provided in Fig. 1. Calibration of the array was conducted using the methods detailed in Gordon et al. [16]. In brief, timing calibrations for both CLOVER and EJ-309 detectors were performed leveraging γ -γ coincidences from a 252Cf spontaneous ﬁssion source. These γ -γ coincidences were also used to obtain

the timing resolution of the HPGe detectors which was, on average, σ = 4.3 ns. One notable deviation from the methods described in Gordon et al. [16] was the establishment of system timing with respect to the neutron beam. There, it was assumed that the photon ﬂash resulting from the deuteron pulse interacting with the thick Carbon break-up target would partially Compton scatter off the thin target in the center of the array, giving rise to a temporally localized signal in the EJ-309 detectors with a shape directly representative of the temporal structure of the deuteron beam. Using data taken with the thin target removed, the contributions from photons scattering off air along the beam path could be subtracted and the radiofrequency (RF) offset could then be calculated using the measured locations of the thin target and detectors. The low Z carbon target did not give rise to appreciable Compton scattering with which to observe this photon ﬂash. Instead, the background from air scattering was modeled using a GEANT4 simulation of the GENESIS array and the cyclotron RF offset timing calibration was determined by comparing the expected γ -ray arrival time from air scattering with the measured data. The observation of the photon ﬂash with the neutron spectrometer (Sec. III) was used to determine the temporal structure of the deuteron beam, which was found to be approximately Gaussian distributed with a full-width at half-maximum of 7.39 ns. Signiﬁcant drift of the RF phase was observed over the course of the experiment. As a result, the data were partitioned into 30-minute intervals and the RF offset was independently determined for each interval. Preliminary γ -ray energy calibrations were evaluated for the HPGe detectors using data collected from a 0.91 µCi 152Eu source. Signiﬁcant gain drift was observed over the duration of the experiment. This was compensated for via application of a set of gain correction scalars identiﬁed by maximizing the cosine similarity [25] between 30-min segments of the data and a reference segment. Then, ﬁnal gain calibrations were conducted using background γ -ray transitions spanning an energy range of 2 to 8 MeV. The efﬁciency of the system was calculated using a previously-validated GEANT4 model of the GENESIS array [16]. The results were evaluated for consistency against the 152Eu source measurements. Figure 2 shows the efﬁciency measured with a 152Eu point source for a representative leaf of the HPGe CLOVER detector positioned at 151◦and the output of a GEANT4 calculation of the efﬁciency using a simulated point source emitting γ rays isotropically with energies uniformly distributed between 0 and 10 MeV. The low-energy efﬁciency is suppressed due to the amplitude-dependent trigger probability of the data acquisition system [16]. The uncertainty on the simulated efﬁciency is primarily due to uncertainty in the trigger probability. For the 4.439 MeV 12C transition, the uncertainty on the simulated efﬁciency for the data shown in Fig. 2 is 3.9%. The detector efﬁciency presented in Fig. 2 was determined under the assumption that the distribution of γ rays from the target was isotropic. To calculate the efﬁciency for a nonisotropically emitting source, the description of the detector efﬁciency was extended to include the initial angle of the source γ ray in the GEANT4 calculation. ## III. NEUTRON FLUX SPECTRUM

The neutron ﬂux spectrum, shown in Fig. 3, was measured using the scatter time-of-ﬂight (sTOF) spectrometer. The experimental conﬁguration of sTOF is described in Ref. [26]. In brief, sTOF was comprised of a 1.27 cm h. x 2.54 cm dia. right circular cylindrical dual-window EJ-309 target scintillator [20] positioned in the neutron beam and four 2.54 cm h. x 2.54 cm dia. right circular cylindrical EJ-309 observation scintillators [20] positioned outside of the beam approximately 0.5 m from the target scintillator at forward angles of approximately 45◦. The dual-window target scintillator cell was coupled to two Hamamatsu H6533 PMTs [21], one on each base, using EJ-550 optical-grade silicone grease [27]. Each single-window observation scintillator cell was coupled to a Hamamatsu H6533 PMT [21] using EJ-550 opticalgrade silicone grease [27]. All PMTs were biased using a

The sTOF spectrometer was ﬁelded downstream of the GENESIS array at a distance of 1007.3 cm from the breakup target. The sTOF neutron spectral ﬂux was extracted using the methods described in Harrig et al. [18] with a few notable deviations. The dual PMT target light and timing were treated as described in Laplace et al. [31]. The gain calibrations and energy-dependent resolutions of the scintillators were determined using in-beam data and the methods outlined in Gordon et al. [16]. The sTOF efﬁciency was calculated using a GEANT4 model of the detector, including the effect of the gas bubble in the EJ-309 scintillator cells (3% by volume), the experimentally determined light yield resolutions [32], and software thresholds used in the analysis of the experimental data. The GEANT4 calculations were performed using the Shielding Physics List [33,34], which uses cross sections from JEFF-3.3 [35] for neutrons below 20 MeV.1 The systematic uncertainty and covariance of the measured ﬂux were determined via a Monte Carlo method akin to that detailed in Brown et al. [36], where the data reduction was repeated using 104 trials in which the measured detector positions, gains, resolutions, timing calibrations, volume percent of the gas bubble, kinematic match window, and software thresholds were sampled about their associated uncertainties. To validate the GEANT4 model of the sTOF efﬁciency, two sets of activation foil packs were ﬁelded over a three-hour irradiation period, one positioned at the center of the GENESIS array and the other at the position of the sTOF target detector. Each foil pack was comprised of natural aluminum, indium, zirconium, and nickel foils of standard density with a diameter

of 5.08 cm and thickness of 0.1 cm. The average of the integrated neutron ﬂux from each of the four foils at the center of the GENESIS array was (2.43 ± 0.02) × 1010 n/(µC sr) and (2.22 ± 0.02) × 1010 n/(µC sr) at the sTOF target position. The relatively lower average integrated neutron ﬂux measured at the sTOF target position is largely due to neutron attenuation in the GENESIS foil pack and intervening air. Taking this into account via GEANT4 modeling, the integrated ﬂux determined using the sTOF spectrometer was (2.23 ± 0.06) × 1010 n/(µC sr), in excellent agreement with the activation foil results. This calculation relied upon an independent measurement of the low-energy neutron ﬂux spectrum obtained using 14 MeV deuterons incident on a carbon breakup target, which was scaled to the neutron ﬂux spectrum measured in this work over the energy range of 3.8 to 4.4 MeV. Based on the agreement between the GEANT4 normalization and the activation foils, only a correction for air attenuation between the target location and the location of sTOF (approx. 2.7 m) was required as a modiﬁcation to the neutron spectral ﬂux used in the determination of the partial γ -ray cross section data.

## IV. DATA ANALYSIS

Events corresponding to the CLOVER detectors were used to construct γ -ray singles time-of-ﬂight (TOF) data. Histograms were constructed for data, where the 12C target was present at the center of the GENESIS array and for the “blank” data (i.e., beam on but no target present). This was accomplished for each CLOVER detector, where signals in multiple leaves of an individual CLOVER detector were accumulated by summing the energy observed in coincident leaf signals (i.e., total-detection mode [23]). Each event in total detection mode was then associated with the closest RF signal observed within the trigger window. These individual events were accumulated into two-dimensional histograms of the γ -ray energy versus the measured time difference, t, between the cyclotron RF signal and the γ -ray event in the HPGe detector minus the γ -ray ﬂight time from the target. That is,

t = ti −tγi −tRF, (3)

where ti is the calibrated time corresponding to a γ -ray event in the ith HPGe detector, tγi is the γ -ray ﬂight time from the carbon scattering target to the ith HPGe detector, and tRF is the time corresponding to the cyclotron RF signal. This measured time difference, t, represents the neutron TOF from the breakup target to the carbon target plus an uncertain number of cyclotron periods. To accumulate a full set of events, histograms were constructed for measured time differences ranging from zero to the cyclotron period. That is, the measured time difference of each event was shifted by an integer multiple of the cyclotron period such that each time difference fell within the range from zero to the cyclotron period. Raw data extracted from a CLOVER functioning in total detection mode are shown in Fig. 4(a). For example, the percent difference between the cross section data obtained in this work and the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation [6] trends from approximately 12% at 9 MeV to approximately 30% at 5.5 MeV. For the ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation, experimental data from Negret

et al. in the energy range of 4.8 to 6.4 MeV were scaled by a constant fraction (reported as 0.87 in Brown et al. [6] and 0.66 in Hale et al. [39], from which the data were adapted) to obtain consistency with R-matrix calculations [6]. However, the results from GENESIS presented here suggest that the magnitude of the ENDF/B-VIII.0 cross section in this energy range (5.5 to 8.5 MeV) is too low. Figures 10(a) and 10(b) show the relative partial γ -ray yields, calculated using Eq. (5), measured at 151.0◦and 122.5◦, respectively, in ratio to the yield measured at 63.0◦. Also plotted are the values for the relative yields calculated from Legendre polynomial ﬁts to the data of Kelly et al. [15] and using the a2 parameters from ENDF/B-VIII.0 [6]. These ratios were also convolved with the angular resolution of the CLOVER detectors to facilitate a proper comparison. The uncertainties in the ratios measured in this work are again dominated by the counting statistics of the background data. The GENESIS data are consistently ∼10% lower than ratios derived from the Kelly etal. measurement. Additionally, many of the features present in the Kelly et al. data, for example the peaks in the 151◦/63◦distribution and dips in the 122.5◦/63◦

distribution around 8 and 10.5 MeV, are not observed in this work. The angular distribution is expected to be highly dependent on the reaction mechanism, e.g., whether it proceeds through a strong resonance or is dominated by other compound processes. The poor energy resolution of the GENESIS data relative to that of Kelly et al. is potentially responsible for the occlusion of these variations. Based upon the symmetry of the angular distribution about 90◦[see Eq. (2)], it is expected that the ratio shown in Fig. 10(b) is close to unity because these detectors were located approximately symmetrically around 90◦. If the a4 term in Eq. (2) is negligible, then the ratio in Fig. 10(a) should be large. The extreme disagreement with ENDF/B-VIII.0 above 8.5 MeV in Fig. 10(a) suggests that the a4 term is not negligible and the ℓ= 2 partial wave plays a signiﬁcant role in the reaction process at these energies. Indeed, this is consistent with the early observations of Wender etal. suggestive of a signiﬁcant a4 term [12]. Future experiments with HPGe detectors placed at these extreme

## VI. SUMMARY

Energy-differential secondary neutrons and γ rays were measured using the GENESIS array following broadspectrum neutron irradiation of a 12C target at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at LBNL. These data were reduced to absolutely normalized partial γ -ray production cross sections using an experimentally benchmarked GEANT4 model of GENESIS for efﬁciency determination. The measured 12C(n, n′ 1γ ) partial γ -ray cross sections were integrated using angular distributions from Kelly et al. [15]. In the region of 11 to 15 MeV, the normalization and shape trend well with angle-integrated scaled shape data from Kelly et al. [11] and ENDF/B-VIII.0 [6]. At lower neutron energy the measured cross section is larger than ENDF/B-VIII.0 by as much as 25%. The relative angular distribution of the 4.439 MeV γ ray agrees

better with state-of-the-art experimental data than the current evaluation.
